summary:
A preview of three November InfoQ online certification cohorts covering production AI systems, retrieval and agent design, engineering team flow, AI roles, and measurement, facilitated by Adi Polak, Lan Chu, and Olimpiu Pop.

story_key: story|title:production ai and engineering team design infoq s november certification cohorts
content_excerpt: A monthly overview of things you need to know as an architect or aspiring architect. Facilitating the Spread of Knowledge and Innovation in Professional Software Development Unlock the full InfoQ experience by logging in! Stay updated with your favorite authors and topics, engage with content, and download exclusive resources. Lily Mara explains how to avoid high-risk software rewrites through incremental FFI refactoring. She shares how engineering teams can replace Python bottlenecks with Rust via PyO3, demonstrating how to achieve dramatic function-level speedups, seamless integration testing, and meaningful infrastructure cost savings without microservice overhead. Agentic LLM systems have moved from linear prompt chains to graph-based workflows and, more recently, code-executing harnesses. Chains are simple but fragile, graphs add branching, retries, and validation, and code harnesses verify outputs through execution. The article advises validating model outputs and choosing the least complex design that meets reliability, speed, and cost needs. Manju Rajashekhar explains how the actor model solves the complex runtime challenges of production AI agents. By treating agents as distributed systems, he discusses state ownership, message passing, write-through state, and supervision boundaries to manage failures, continuations, and mutable execution graphs, moving agentic workflows beyond fragile demos to resilient architecture. Nathen Harvey shares insights from DORA research on AI adoption in software delivery. He explains why AI acts as an amplifier, how the DORA AI Capabilities Model drives outcomes, and why engineering leaders must evolve beyond bottlenecks like code reviews to achieve sustainable productivity, reduce delivery instability, and empower developers without burning out their teams. Andrew Martin discusses why AI security is fundamentally tied to Kubernetes security. He shares insights into the evolving AI threat landscape, covering non-deterministic agent behavior, GPU supply chain vulnerabilities, shared compute risks, and practical defense strategies - from prompt firewalling to agentic identity - to help secure cloud-native AI workloads in production environments. Secure and govern production AI systems, from sensitive data to guardrails, evals, and audits. Online. Register now. title: Conservative Meta-Agent Search: Architecture Adaptation under Non-Stationarity
summary: Automated agentic-system design is typically evaluated on static task suites with immediate scalar rewards. Deployed systems face persistent shift, delayed dependent feedback, correlated component failures, and costly architecture changes. We formalize meta-agent architecture search as sequential incumbent replacement with switching costs and hard risk constraints and introduce Conservative Meta-Agent Search (CMAS). CMAS retrieves archived architectures and proposes typed graph edits, then scores each against the incumbent by paired shadow replay under common random numbers, with interventional component credit. Promotion requires an empirically calibrated, variance-penalized simultaneous score above a pre-specified margin, and is followed by a simulated canary stage and pre-specified rollback. Since backtests cannot certify meta-level skill, we introduce MetaInvest-Bench, a regime-switching simulator whose specified worker competence makes a surrogate-optimal architecture computable, with leakage-controlled replay, adversarial governance tracks, and five negative controls. Financial streams serve as a risk-sensitive testbed for meta-level generalization; we claim no alpha. Across 96 streams, CMAS cuts normalized mean surrogate dynamic-oracle regret from 0.116 to 0.104 and raises held-out utility from 0.44 to 0.48 over the strongest adaptive baseline; when extra workers add no value, it contracts to near-single-agent teams. Its deployment inference cost is ~6% lower, though its search-inclusive token cost is the highest of the methods compared. The observed per-update false-promotion rate is 3.4% against a nominal 5% target, and 4.8% in a sealed rerun. The calibration is empirical: it concerns an update-level replay statistic on an author-designed benchmark, and guarantees neither full-utility improvement, nor absence of simulated canary-stage harm, nor sequence-level error control.

title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
summary: Tool-using language model agents rely on environmental facts to decide whether an action is permitted. When a tool response omits a safety-relevant fact, an agent may carry out a prohibited action even though the user request is benign and every returned statement is true. We introduce \bench{}, an executable benchmark for evaluating unsafe execution, safety boundaries, and evidence recovery in LLM agents under missing evidence. It contains 300 matched unsafe/safe task pairs across six domains. By systematically suppressing critical facts, the benchmark measures unsafe execution under critical evidence omission and determines the minimum observed failure cardinality, including failures with full evidence and cases with no observed failure after exhaustive testing. An independent audit tool tests whether agents seek missing facts and then withhold prohibited actions while completing permissible tasks. The benchmark reveals substantial variation across the ten models in omission robustness, evidence acquisition, and appropriate action. Resistance to missing evidence does not necessarily translate into useful recovery. Recovery access reduces unsafe execution for all ten models, but agents differ in whether they actively obtain the missing facts and use them to act appropriately in both worlds.

title: When LLMs Forget What They Believe: Characterizing State Integrity Collapse in Long-Horizon Dialogues
summary: Large language models can repeat an instruction while failing to keep obeying it. We study this recall-compliance dissociation in long-horizon dialogue and define State Integrity Collapse: a model preserves a stated constraint in memory but stops applying it to later turns. We introduce StateTrack-Bench, a controlled suite of conversations covering numerical, format, role/persona, factual-memory, and logical-rule constraints. Across seven provider-pinned model snapshots and five dialogue-depth probes, strict joint retention ranges from 62.4% to 100.0%, with degradation concentrated in symbolic constraints and in one especially brittle model. A forked recall audit shows that 88.6% of observed failures are behavioral-drift failures rather than ordinary forgetting; excluding the brittle outlier preserves this diagnosis (84.4% of failures). Extended evaluations at depths up to 50 turns confirm that the dissociation persists beyond the core benchmark, while Structured State Anchoring recovers up to 24.4 points on immutable constraints. The results show that reliability cannot be inferred from single-turn instruction following alone; evaluation must track whether remembered constraints remain operational as dialogue state grows. Code and artifacts are available at: https://github.com/xzzvsxd/StateTrack.

title: Introducing our Training API
summary: Spindle is an open-source API for training and fine-tuning open models — deploy a server with a single command and run any Tinker-compatible training code against it.
content_excerpt: Thinking Machines’ Tinker changed how people do post-training. You write the training loop in plain Python on your laptop, and Tinker runs the forward and backward passes on its GPUs. We’re big fans, and so are many of the teams we work with. We think a good API deserves more than one implementation. Today we’re releasing Spindle , an open-source, Tinker-compatible training server that runs in your Modal workspace. Because you own the server, you can customize anything in it, and you pay for GPU time instead of tokens. Our default configs are tuned to maximize GPU utilization out of the box, and we plan to keep shipping optimizations to push price-performance further. Modal now covers the whole post-training stack, from on-demand clusters to a library that runs the loop for you. Where do you start? If you’d rather not write a training loop, use our training library, Modal Dojo , which we released yesterday. Simply bring a model and a dataset, and Dojo will handle the rest. If you want to own everything down to the cluster, Modal gives you the raw primitives: on-demand multi-node clusters and sandboxes for RL rollouts . Spindle sits in between. You write the training loop with your own losses, rewards, and environments, and Spindle handles the distributed training underneath it. It supports full-parameter training and multi-LoRA on a wide range of open models. For teams running many experiments, Spindle supports hundreds of concurrent training runs at similar performance and significantly reduced cost compared to closed-source APIs. Spindle’s Tinker-compatible API is backed by a distributed control plane that handles request and session management, and container autoscaling built on Modal Functions . Spindle’s backend features a set of disaggregated trainer engines and inference pools. Note that they don’t have to run on the same accelerators or precisions! We’ve written about how to keep RL stable in these cases and take advantage of the inherent cost savings and higher GPU availability. Our whole system is built on top of Modal primitives: Modal Clusters enable incoming requests for large-models to be scheduled on dynamically-available RDMA-connected nodes without requiring a cluster reservation, Modal Volumes provide fast, durable checkpointing, and Modal Servers provide a fast inference layer. While building multi-LoRA training, we’ve also upstreamed various improvements to Miles and SGLang , and we’ll continue investing in the open-source ecosystem. De

title: Context Engineering (Agent Memory) for AI Agents Starts with Retrieval
summary: Agents waste time and context on clumsy searches, oversized results and stale data. Learn the retrieval techniques LangChain's Deep Agents harness uses to get the right context in.
story_key: story|title:context engineering agent memory for ai agents starts with retrieval
content_excerpt: Imagine you’re taking an open book exam: you technically have all the answers, but somehow that makes it even harder to find the right one. Hand an agent a question and it’s left with a similar predicament: it has a limited context window, so like us humans, it has to retrieve information to complete certain tasks (instead of having everything memorized). When searching, agents struggle with: Luckily, there are several techniques at an agent’s disposal that allow it to retrieve the correct information. It’s the job of an agent harness to apply these techniques strategically to get the model the right context at the right time for the given task. This blog covers the challenges with agent retrieval (finding and pulling in only the information necessary for the task at hand), the techniques at our disposal to combat them, and how to keep these in mind when designing an agent harness (using LangChain’s Deep Agents harness as an example). For more on how to manage context once it's in the context window, check out this blog on Context Engineering . Let’s see how this can be applied in a real-world use case: a competitive analysis agent. Every Monday, an agent researches hundreds of competitors and writes a report in the team's template. It needs to: Each of these is a different kind of retrieval and therefore faces different problems. We've built our agent using the Deep Agents harness so there are a few techniques that we can apply out of the box to minimize these problems. Our agent has to find three things for each competitor. If each one takes a dozen tries (opening files just to see what's inside, or rewording a search because the source uses different words), its context window fills up with failed searches before it even writes a word of the report. Therefore, the best search is the one the agent doesn't have to repeat, and that means using the right tool for each job. One of the most common ways for an agent to search through information is with a filesystem. However, if our agent opens every file to see what's inside, it's searching very inefficiently: each file it reads lands in its context window, so it can fill up just from looking. A better approach is to check names and keywords first (the way you'd scan a book's index instead of reading every page during an open-book exam). title: Do "True" and "False" Add Up to One? Complement Consistency in LLM-Agent Opinion Simulations
summary: In LLM-agent opinion simulations, each agent reports the probability that a claim is true after seeing its own previous probability and the probabilities reported by its neighbors, and that number becomes its state in the next round. If the number describes the agent's position rather than the sentence it was shown, then rewriting the claim as its complement and replacing every probability p with 1 - p should return the complementary answer, so the two reports should sum to one. We test this with three small open models: Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.2-3B and Gemma-3-4B. On 2,304 agent states taken from a running network simulation, Qwen's paired reports sum to 1.18 on average, and on 48 real fact-checking claims from AVeriTeC they again exceed one. A controlled benchmark of 24 worlds, each with exactly two possible outcomes, shows the same failure in all three models. The discrepancy is two to ten times larger than the change produced by a same-meaning paraphrase, and it persists under repeated sampling and across peer group sizes and report strengths. When the reports are fed back into two populations that start from complementary states, the populations do not remain mirror images: their divergence is positive after five rounds for every model. Averaging each answer with the complement of its paired answer restores consistency by construction and lowers Brier loss averaged over the two wordings, but at the final round it beats the better of the two original wordings for only one of the three models. A schedule-by-targeting experiment on the same model gives a small, stable interaction because such sweeps keep the claim wording fixed. Consistency under rewording therefore needs its own test before simulated probabilities are read as beliefs

title: J-Comm: Jacobian-Guided Latent Communication between LLM Agents
summary: Latent communication requires both an effective continuous reasoning process and an interface through which an external model can leverage its intermediate computation. We present J-Comm, a framework comprising two core components. First, a training-free Geometric Agreement for Latent Reasoning (GEAR) reweights token candidates over existing model embeddings, which monotonically optimizes geometric consensus among candidate tokens in embedding space at each step. Second, we introduce an H+J (Hidden-and-Jacobian) communication interface that gives the Receiver two complementary views of the Sender's reasoning. The H channel supplies continuous inputs derived from feedback distributions, while the J channel conveys intermediate-state cues in vocabulary-indexed Jacobian-lens coordinates. Intuitively, H provides inputs for the Receiver to reason from, while J offers additional guidance within its computation. The Receiver reconstructs these cues using its own dictionary and injects them into intermediate layers during prefill, enabling communication without sharing key-value caches or requiring identical model widths. In Qwen3-8B to Qwen3-4B communication, J-Comm achieves the highest mean score across seven benchmarks, including 94.80% on MATH500, 54.55% on GPQA-Diamond, 73.33% on AIME2024+2025, and 62.93% success on ALFWorld. Compared with TextMAS, it improves performance by 1.29-8.59 percentage points and reduces generated text tokens by 19.2-74.8%.

title: Introducing vLLM TorchTPU
summary: vllm-torchtpu is a new vLLM backend for Google Cloud TPUs built on TorchTPU, with Pallas kernels, multi-host parallelism, KV cache offloading, and disaggregated serving.
content_excerpt: Today we're releasing vLLM TorchTPU ( vllm-torchtpu ), a new backend for running vLLM on Google Cloud TPUs. It's built on Google's TorchTPU stack and runs the model definitions that already live in vLLM, so most models that work in vLLM today can be served on TPU without changes to the model code. This work comes out of the engineering partnership between Inferact and Google we announced last month. Our goals for the project are to: vllm-torchtpu is an out-of-tree vLLM platform plugin. Once installed, vLLM picks it up automatically through the vllm.platform_plugins entry point. Models run through vLLM's standard model runner and are compiled with torch.compile(backend="tpu") , which lowers to XLA. Each TPU device gets its own worker process, the same way vLLM runs on GPUs, and communication between devices goes through torch.distributed . This means the scheduler, workers, KV cache manager, and API server are all unmodified upstream vLLM. The TPU-specific work sits underneath them, mostly in a set of JAX/Pallas kernels that are registered as custom ops and called from inside the compiled graph. This requires Python 3.12 on a Cloud TPU VM, and installs a matching vLLM, torch , torch_tpu , and libtpu alongside the plugin. The installation guide also covers uv , source builds, and Docker . The first startup compiles TPU graphs for the configured shapes, which can take a few minutes. Set VLLM_XLA_CACHE_PATH to reuse compiled artifacts across restarts (see Compilation & Warmup Cache ). Speculative decoding, prefix caching, multi-LoRA, structured outputs, and multimodal inputs are all enabled with the usual vLLM flags. See the quickstart for more examples, including offline batch inference, multimodal models, and multi-LoRA. vllm-torchtpu uses custom Pallas kernels for complex operations that benefit from hand-tuning on TPU. Some examples: We've focused heavily on the workloads that put the most pressure on serving systems today, especially multi-turn agentic and multimodal traffic, where contexts keep growing and tool outputs can be long. All six of vLLM's parallelism dimensions are supported, on both single-host and multi-host TPU slices, and they can be combined: For large MoE models, we usually get the best throughput from data-parallel attention with expert parallelism (for example, DP=8, TP=1 with EP on a single v7x host). This keeps attention local to each device and spreads the experts across the whole slice. For long contexts, PCP and DCP split prefill

title: claude-code v2.1.307
summary:
What's changed

  • Added /claude-api api-version to move Claude API code to API version 2026-10-21
  • Added the claude_code.safety_event OpenTelemetry event for each tool call a permission rule, auto mode, a safety check, a hook or the sandbox stopped, prompted or sent back
  • Fixed requests failing with a model-not-found error when CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT is set and the model is an alias with the [1m] suffix, such as opus[1m]
  • Fixed the prompt-caching-scope beta header being sent behind custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL gateways and on Foundry, where it has no effect
  • Fixed MCP servers showing "needs authentication" in claude -p on macOS while the login keychain was locked; they now say why, and the next run after an unlock connects without a new sign-in
  • Fixed MCP servers being reported as timed out, and staying failed in headless runs, when a macOS or Linux computer went to sleep while they were connecting
  • Fixed HTTP MCP tool calls being sent twice when the connection closed mid-call; only read-only or idempotent tools are now retried
  • Fixed a turn sometimes starting without an SDK MCP server's latest tools when a background task was running
  • Fixed some "Autocompact is thrashing" errors in turns that read many PDF pages, images or other large tool results
  • Fixed /autocompact in cloud sessions going back to the default window after the session restarted
  • Fixed a conversation cleared with /clear sometimes coming back when a cloud or self-hosted runner session restarted
  • Fixed CLAUDE_STREAM_FIRST_BYTE_TIMEOUT_MS being ignored in Claude apps gateway sessions
  • Fixed telemetry from Claude Desktop sessions behind a Claude apps gateway being rejected when OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS is set
  • Fixed /permissions > Recently denied not showing the denied shell command, and auto mode's local classifier ignoring an approval from there when it checks a retried command; approving a row now names the command, not its description
  • Fixed /help and the / command menu showing long model-facing descriptions for bundled skills such as /claude-api instead of their short descriptions
  • Fixed subagent transcripts recording placeholder token usage and an empty stop reason for streamed responses
  • Fixed model switches through the Agent SDK's setModel(), and apps built on it, being refused when the API took more than 5 seconds to confirm the model; Claude Code now waits up to 15 seconds
  • Fixed a background command stopped through a connected app (such as the desktop app archiving an idle session) being reported to Claude as stopped by the user; the notice now names its output file
  • Fixed WebFetch in Cowork cloud sessions reporting a tool error when a site answered with a 4xx status or a robots.txt refusal; it is now a normal result, as in local sessions
  • Fixed write tools on a directly configured GitHub MCP server showing a form that closed without creating anything in the desktop app's Code tab
  • Fixed Artifact tool reads failing with a connection reset when the server had closed a reused connection
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed sessions with --use-anthropic-git-proxy committing a .claude/settings.local.json left in the clone by an earlier session
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed archiving or requeueing a session, or stopping the runner, during its checkout hook leaving the hook's processes running and the runner's slot held
  • Improved recovery from unparseable tool calls: Claude Code now retries the call up to twice before ending the turn with an error
  • Improved fork subagents launched together: each is now told which launch is its own, so forks are much less likely to try to start each other's work
  • Improved browser sign-in: the success page now appears as soon as sign-in completes, without waiting for your account profile to load
  • Improved web search errors in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions: a search refused with a 403 that gives a reason now shows that reason instead of a generic "Authentication error"
  • Improved the time to the first reply in cloud sessions when one of the desktop app's MCP servers can't connect
  • Improved Remote Control connect time for sessions whose transcript contains large pasted images or PDF reads
  • Changed the notice Claude gets when the WebSearch budget is used up to also tell it not to query search engines in a browser or through computer use
  • Changed the axScreenReader setting and CLAUDE_AX_SCREEN_READER in a settings env block to apply only from user, managed or --settings settings (since 2.1.305)
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed checkout hooks to be stopped after 30 minutes by default, failing the session's setup; if yours needs longer, raise --checkout-hook-timeout-min or set it to 0
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed the certificate file built for Anthropic-managed git to filter its trusted certificates as the CLI does; a [runner:warn] line gives the number left out
  • [VSCode] Added a notice on the microphone button when voice dictation stops by itself (15 seconds without recognized speech, or the 2-minute limit), saying why and that the text so far is kept
  • [VSCode] Fixed a long prompt expanded with Show more covering the whole chat panel: a pinned prompt is now capped at 40% of the panel and scrolls
  • [VSCode] Fixed part of a list item or table cell with LaTeX math pasting as a new list or table in rich text editors
  • [VSCode] Fixed dictation failing behind a TLS-inspecting proxy when NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS is set only in ~/.claude/settings.json; it now also follows CLAUDE_CODE_CERT_STORE
  • [VSCode] Changed the "still open somewhere else" notice to also cover a Claude process left over from an extension restart, which usually ends on its own within about 10 minutes
  • [VSCode] Changed voice dictation to filter its trusted certificates as the CLI does
  • [VSCode] Changed the extension's own requests to filter their trusted certificates as the CLI does, and to trust the NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS file named in the environment or in user settings
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the repository picker saying "No repositories match" while a search was still running; it now shows "Searching…" until the results arrive
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the "Waiting for a runner" status on self-hosted environments being cut off; with on-demand runners it now counts up from your last message and shows failed attempts
  • [Code Review] Added @claude review stop (also off and pause) to Code Review, ending an @claude review always subscription on a pull request without starting a new review

title: Expanding Claude availability and deployment choice on Google Cloud
summary:
Every organization has unique requirements for building and scaling generative AI. At Google Cloud, we are committed to giving developers model choice and architectural flexibility to run workloads however they need.

Today, we’re announcing the general availability of an Anthropic-managed deployment option for Claude Models on Google Cloud. This gives teams more choice in how they run their models, helping them consolidate AI workloads on Google Cloud alongside our existingGoogle-managed deployment option. 

Both options deliver the same frontier models on day zero, the same pricing, and the same Google Cloud billing. The difference comes down to who acts as your data processor and whether you need access to the new Claude platform features when they launch:

[NEW] Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed)

Delivers day-zero access to Claude models and Claude Platform features such as Claude Managed Agents (beta), skills, and code execution. Anthropic operates the stack as the data processor on Google Cloud infrastructure under Anthropic’s terms of service, while organizations authenticate with Google Cloud IAM, maintain Cloud Audit Logging, and consolidate spend under their existing Google Cloud billing and eligible commitments.

Learn more: Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic-managed).

Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed)

Continues to deliver day-zero access to the latest Claude models with strict governance, compliance, and sovereignty requirements. Google Cloud operates as the data processor under existing customer agreements, providing VPC Service Controls, Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK), and data residency in the U.S., EU, and APAC. New Claude Platform features roll out over time as they are integrated into the Google-managed infrastructure. Teams also benefit from native integrations with Google Cloud services like BigQuery and Model Armor, along with standard billing and eligible commitment drawdown. 

Learn more: Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed)

Comparing deployment options

 

Feature

Anthropic-managed

Google-managed

Model availability

Available on Day 0

Pricing & commitments

Standard pricing (draws down eligible Google Cloud commitments)

No matter how you choose to deploy, you can access Anthropic's latest frontier models on Google Cloud, including Claude Fable 5.1, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, and Opus 5.5, with new platform features available immediately on the Anthropic-managed option and rolling out on the Google-managed option once integrated. This gives developers the full spectrum of reasoning, coding, and multi-modal capabilities with Google Cloud IAM and Marketplace billing. Get started.
